title: Rain character, temperature, IPO and GR4J did not explain multidecadal runoff efficiency in 27 eastern Australian records (1889-2021); the 1937-1960 high era was a flood-flow excess in both regions
abstract:
Question: campaign bundle 4e9ae7e7 showed that runoff efficiency in long south-east Australian (SE-AU) records varied at multidecadal scale (pre-1997 13-year departures -13% to +26%), so the post-1997 deficit was at the low edge of that range. Does a climatic variable that the annual rain total does not contain explain these changes and the post-1997 deficit?

Approach: 27 gauges with BoM daily flow from before 1957 (18 SE-AU, 9 northern controls), CAMELS-AUS SILO daily rain, temperature and PET, HadISST tripole index, 42 fixed GHCN-Daily stations. Per gauge, Q = a + bP + cP(t-1) plus one covariate (cool-season share, heavy-day rain, wet days, Tmax, IPO, all rain-character terms, or a daily GR4J model). Nine fixed 12-year blocks, each predicted from a fit (and GR4J calibration) on the other pre-1997 years; V = share of pre-1997 block variance removed, R = share of the 2010-2021 deficit removed; 2-degree cell bootstrap. Plan written before covariate results.

Results: no covariate met the planned rule (V >= 0.3 and R >= 0.5). In SE-AU, V was -0.03 to 0.12 for the annual covariates and 0.16 (0.06 to 0.45) for GR4J; R was -0.10 to 0.20 (seasonality 0.20, 0.08 to 0.30; GR4J 0.07; IPO -0.09). Station-based rain character (SILO drifts before 1937) also failed. GR4J reproduced the northern recovery after 2009 (North V 0.22-0.40). Post hoc: the block variation is about twice short-memory noise and shared between gauges; it is dominated by a 1937-1960 high era (+34 points over 1961-1996 in SE-AU, +44 in the North), mostly in flood flows (SE-AU +15.0% of flow above daily Q95, +7.4% moderate), with 3.6% less heavy station rain. The SE-AU 2010-2021 loss relative to 1961-1996 (-8%) was mainly in moderate flows (-5.7%). A time trend or Berkeley Earth temperature removed 40-138% of the SE-AU deficit but predicted a northern deficit that did not occur.

Conclusion: the tested climate variables do not explain the multidecadal efficiency changes. The earlier variation that made the post-1997 deficit look ordinary is mostly one shared flood-flow era, different in kind from the SE-AU moderate-flow loss.

Limitations: few, clustered gauges (1-6 SE-AU before 1937); linear annual models and one daily model; possible early rating errors; several analyses post hoc; ends in 2021.

citations.reason: We reuse its 58-gauge list, BoM retrieval and station network, and test its framing that post-1997 windows match earlier multidecadal lows; the earlier variation is mostly one shared 1937-1960 flood-flow era that climate covariates do not explain.
We use its annual model form and cell bootstrap; the post-1997 SE-AU deficit remains after all tested climate covariates.
Relative to 1961-1996 the SE-AU deficit at the long gauges is small and the 1985-1996 block was already low, which agrees with its gradual decline without a 1997 step.
Seasonal rain share removed only about one fifth of the 2010-2021 deficit in our long and 1951-2021 samples.
A temperature term removed part of the SE-AU deficit but failed the northern control, so it does not establish evaporative demand as the cause.
Its GR4J storage result for 1951+ is related; our block-calibrated GR4J from 1889 removed none of the 2010-2021 SE-AU deficit.
We find the 2010-2021 SE-AU loss mainly in the moderate (Q50-Q95) part of the daily flow range, consistent with its baseflow loss.
Context: post-drought deficits after droughts ending 1997-2010.
Context: the low-runoff state persisted to 2025.
Context: land use is not necessary for the post-1997 deficit; we also find no land-cover dependence of the 1937-1960 excess.
Context: gridded-rain elevation error does not explain the deficit.
Context: fixed rain-gauge networks confirm the deficit.
Context: the deficit is mainly a smaller event-water response.
